query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In‐situ substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder will moderate rapid cooling rates, reducing thermal gradients and promoting uniform elemental diffusion, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity over conventional processing by minimizing segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation through improved thermal management.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi high‐entropy alloy powder feedstock that, when processed by conventional additive manufacturing or bulk techniques, tends to develop compositional segregation, high residual stresses, and defect-laden microstructures due to rapid cooling.
generation.intervention: Implement in-situ substrate preheating during the additive manufacturing process (e.g., using a moderately heated build platform).
generation.conditions: The intervention applies during laser additive manufacturing (such as direct energy deposition or powder bed fusion) using typical energy density and scanning settings, with the substrate temperature maintained at a moderate level throughout the build.
generation.structural_mediator: A more homogeneous melt pool that cools more gradually, resulting in refined and uniform grains with reduced elemental segregation and diminished residual stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate reduces the thermal gradient between the melt pool and the underlying layers, which moderates cooling-induced stresses and limits compositional segregation by promoting uniform elemental diffusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed AlCrFeNiSi with no substrate preheat, the preheated samples should exhibit lower residual stress levels, diminished compositional segregation (as evidenced by more uniform elemental distribution), fewer defects such as cracks or porosity, and improved overall mechanical integrity. There is some risk that excessive preheating might slightly reduce yield strength due to grain coarsening, but within an optimized temperature window (~300 °C), the benefits should prevail.
generation.baseline: Conventional additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi without substrate preheating, which typically shows significant segregation, higher residual stresses, and defect formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under typical laser additive manufacturing conditions (e.g., similar laser power, scan speeds, and layer thickness) and for powders of comparable composition and particle size distribution. It may not directly extend to vastly different processing methods (e.g., bulk casting) or significantly altered thermal management environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheating temperature and its balance between reducing thermal gradients versus avoiding adverse grain growth need precise experimental calibration. Also, while reduced residual stresses and segregations are anticipated, their quantitative reduction relative to mechanical performance improvements is yet to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using an identical laser additive manufacturing process: one set with the substrate preheated to ~300 °C and a control set with no preheating. Ensure all other processing parameters are kept constant.
measurements: Residual stress measurements (e.g., via X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction)
Microstructural analysis (grain size, phase homogeneity, elemental mapping using SEM/EDS)
Mechanical testing (tensile strength, hardness, fracture toughness, and defect density assessment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical integrity (e.g., reduced residual stress, lower defect density, or more uniform microstructure) compared to the non-preheated ones, or if they exhibit inferior mechanical properties, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. Additively manufactured H13 typically solidifies into a martensitic matrix with retained austenite and carbides, but the steep thermal gradients and cyclic reheating between layers cause high residual stresses, porosity, and cracking; hence, the routine relies on post-build stress relief and tempering. While substrate preheating and in situ thermal management are well established in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), comparable strategies remain far less explored in DED/LENS® because most systems lack tightly integrated, high-temperature platform control and studies have focused on parameter windows or post-deposition heat treatments.
